findings.description: The application fails to send the X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff header, allowing legacy browsers (IE, older Chrome) to perform MIME‑sniffing on responses. This can cause the browser to interpret a response as a different content type, potentially enabling cross‑site scripting or data leakage if the content is maliciously crafted.

findings.description: The site sends a Content‑Security‑Policy header that sets "default-src 'none'" but omits directives that do not inherit from default‑src, such as "frame‑ancestors" and "form‑action". Because these directives are missing, the browser treats them as if they were not present, effectively allowing framing and form submissions to any origin. This misconfiguration can enable click‑jacking, phishing, or credential‑stealing attacks even though the default source is restrictive.

Content Security Policy (CSP) is an added layer of security that helps to detect and mitigate certain types of attacks, including Cross Site Scripting (XSS) and data injection attacks. These attacks are used for everything from data theft to site defacement or distribution of malware. CSP provides a set of standard HTTP headers that allow website owners to declare approved sources of content that browsers should be allowed to load on that page — covered types are JavaScript, CSS, HTML frames, fonts, images and embeddable objects such as Java applets, ActiveX, audio and video files. Ensure that your web server, application server, load balancer, etc. is configured to set the Content-Security-Policy header. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CSP
